answer.explanation: Redis is configured with maxmemory=8MB and policy noeviction. The API is caching per-session blobs under keys like cache:session:N with no TTL (ttl=-1), and each of these blobs is ~450KB. With ~24 such keys already resident, used_memory (~12.2MB) has exceeded maxmemory, and redis has been over the limit for a sustained period (current_eviction_exceeded_time≈96ms accumulated, growing). Because the policy is noeviction, redis refuses new writes once over the memory cap, returning OOM errors (errorstat_OOM count=21 and rising) instead of evicting old data. The POST /jobs handler tries to RPUSH the job onto the 'jobs' queue in redis; when that RPUSH gets an OOM error, the API falls back to processing the job synchronously in-process (which takes ~2s) instead of the normal <5ms enqueue-and-return-202 path, exactly matching the observed jump from 3ms/202 to ~2020-2034ms/200 on every POST /jobs after the first request. The worker and queue length (llen jobs = 0) are otherwise healthy/idle, confirming jobs are no longer being enqueued at all -- the latency is coming from the API's synchronous fallback path caused by redis write failures, not from worker slowness or DB/API resource contention.
answer.suggested_fix: Immediately raise redis maxmemory (or switch policy to an eviction policy like allkeys-lru) to stop the OOM condition, and fix the API to set a reasonable TTL/expiry on cache:session:* keys (and/or stop caching large blobs per-session) so memory usage stays bounded. Also add alerting on redis used_memory vs maxmemory and on OOM error counts, and make the API's job-enqueue fallback path explicit/observable (log a warning and emit a metric) instead of silently degrading to synchronous processing so this failure mode is caught before it manifests only as latency.
